implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the contract, not a new mechanism: a discriminated union of part kinds forces the router's switch to be exhaustive, so every element type has exactly one processor, and the aggregation is typed against the part results. The realization remains parts.map(route) + await Promise.all + reduce, with the result array's input order as the correlation state; the classic aggregator object is unnecessary in-process.
pitfalls: A non-exhaustive switch on the part union compiles only if the return type is widened; keep the exhaustiveness check (never/assertNever) so a new part kind cannot silently fall through.
Promise.all's rejection still does not cancel the losing parts - model failure in the result type (Result/partial aggregate) instead of relying on exceptions.

variants.name: node:worker_threads pool fan-in (CPU-bound parts)
variants.idiom_name: Worker pool + Promise per postMessage + reduce
variants.implementation_notes: For CPU-bound parts, node:worker_threads executes JavaScript in parallel on real threads; the docs recommend a pool because worker creation overhead otherwise exceeds the benefit, and note that workers share memory only by transferring ArrayBuffers or SharedArrayBuffer. The splitter posts one part per pool slot, each post's promise is the part future, and Promise.all plus a reduce aggregates; the worker's reply carries the part index, which is the correlation state that survives structured cloning.
pitfalls: Workers do not share ordinary objects: parts are structured-cloned, so functions, class instances and promises are lost - pass plain data or transfer buffers.
One worker per part spawns a thread per element (the Node docs warn the overhead dwarfs short tasks); use a pool and terminate it on shutdown or the process will not exit.
Errors inside a worker arrive as an 'error' event, not as a rejected promise from postMessage; the pool must reject the part's promise or the composite hangs.
